name: The Angel of Power 2 Wins (Mathe)
description:
## Motivation

The **Angel problem** asks whether a piece with a bounded movement range can survive forever on an infinite chessboard while an adversary destroys one square per turn. A large movement range does not settle the question by itself: the adversary may destroy squares far ahead of the moving piece, and no fixed finite board represents all possible plays. The problem therefore combines local geometric restrictions with an infinite strategic requirement. Its formalization provides a concrete setting in which the order of strategic quantifiers and the distinction between finite and infinite play both matter.

This project concerns a published solution, not a new solution to an open conjecture. Andras Mathe proved that power two suffices in [The Angel of power 2 wins](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548306008303), published in 2007. The source for this mission is that paper, specifically its definitions in Section 2 and the power-two result in Section 4. The manuscript's internal page numbers run from 1 to 9; they differ from the journal's pages 363-374. The principal target is Theorem 4.6 on manuscript page 8.

## Setting

A **square** is an integer pair in the infinite lattice. The Angel starts at the origin. A move of power $p$ changes each coordinate by at most $p$ in absolute value. Intermediate squares do not constrain a jump. The formalization follows the source's finite-journey convention, which permits zero-length moves. The Devil moves first, and on each turn chooses a square to eat or passes. The Angel then chooses a destination using the observed history. Landing on any previously eaten square, including the square eaten on that turn, loses. The source permits the Devil to name the occupied square; this does not itself end the game before the Angel's next landing.

A strategy is a function of information already revealed. It cannot inspect future opposing actions. Devil strategies take the finite list of visited squares. Angel strategies take that list together with the finite list of Devil actions, including the action on the current turn. Recursion on the number of completed rounds produces a unique play for each pair of strategies. Losing continuations remain formally defined, but are not counted as surviving plays.

A **Nice Devil** is restricted by the Angel's earlier opportunities. The origin is protected, as is every square within movement range of any visited position before the last position in the current history. This is the restriction used in equation (2) of the paper. Against this restricted opponent, merely staying alive is not the intended objective. The Angel must reach positions outside every finite box centred at the origin. No single bounded region may contain the entire play.

## Formalization targets

The main target is Theorem 4.6:

$$\exists A\;\forall D,\quad \operatorname{Survives}(2,A,D).$$

Here $A$ and $D$ range over the history-dependent strategies just described, and survival requires legal, uneaten landings at every round. The existential quantifier over $A$ precedes the universal quantifier over $D$: choosing a different prescient Angel strategy separately for each opponent would not state the target.

The two initial milestones correspond to the paper's main division. Theorem 2.7 supplies a Nice Devil confinement consequence when the Angel has no winning strategy, with the determinacy observation in the introduction included in that formulation. Confinement applies to every finite safe prefix, not merely to plays that already survive forever. Theorem 4.5 supplies a power-two Angel strategy that survives and reaches outside every finite box against every Nice Devil. These milestones retain the infinite-board and unrestricted-history quantifiers.

## Significance

The mathematical result gives a fixed movement range sufficient to withstand an adversary operating anywhere on the board. Its conclusion is uniform in the opponent and in the duration of play. A finite simulation, however long, cannot supply that conclusion. Nor does a strategy that succeeds against one chosen Devil establish it against all Devils.

The formalization aims to make the game's conventions, the reduction to the restricted opponent, and the geometric escape argument separately inspectable. The current development contains the game definitions and small checked foundational lemmas. The paper's principal results are open formalization targets. In particular, a proved logical lemma assembling the two milestones does not prove either milestone. The project makes no claim of a completed machine-checked solution at this stage.

## Difficulty

The principal obstacles are strategic and geometric. Finite survival statements must support the infinite strategic conclusion without exchanging quantifiers. Restrictions on the Nice Devil must protect exactly the squares specified by the source. In the geometric part, the source's wall-following construction must remain legal while the obstacle configuration changes, and its boundary estimates must connect to actual plays. A numerical contradiction between perimeter bounds is useful only after those bounds have been established for the constructed strategy. These are mathematical obligations, not consequences of successful type checking of the model.

## Formalization scope

The initial Lean implementation uses integer coordinate pairs, finite lists, optional Devil actions, and primitive recursion on natural numbers. It is pinned to Lean 4.33.1, matching the selected platform environment. The current files use Lean's standard library; Mathlib can be introduced at the platform's pinned revision when geometric infrastructure requires it. There is no finite-board cutoff and no assumed winning strategy inside the definitions.

The first proposal contains one shared definition bundle, two theorem milestones, and the main theorem. Further decomposition of the milestones will be added only after the corresponding geometric or strategy interfaces are precisely stated and audited. Expected remaining work includes the finite-journey reduction, the compactness/determinacy connection, connected-square boundary estimates from Claim 4.2, and the wall-following construction underlying Proposition 4.3. The present scope is the integer-power Angel game through Theorem 4.6; the fractional-speed King extension in Section 5 is excluded.

## Selected references

- Andras Mathe, *The Angel of power 2 wins*, Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 16 (2007), 363-374. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548306008303).
- [Archived author manuscript](https://web.archive.org/web/20161013034302id_/http://homepages.warwick.ac.uk/~masibe/angel-mathe.pdf), Sections 2 and 4, especially Theorems 2.7, 4.5 and 4.6.

main_theorem.theorem_title: Theorem 4.6: the Angel of power two wins
main_theorem.natural_language_statement: There exists a single power-two Angel strategy that makes legal uneaten landings forever against every Devil strategy on the infinite integer lattice, with the Devil moving first and permitted to pass.
